title: Delirium: recognising it, finding the cause, and what not to give

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the American Geriatrics Society postoperative delirium guideline and NICE delirium guidance. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Which two features must both be present for delirium on the Confusion Assessment Method?
a: Acute onset with a fluctuating course
questions.why: Plus either disorganised thinking or an altered level of consciousness. Inattention is tested by asking for the months backwards or a digit span, not by orientation questions.

questions.q: Which form of delirium is most common and most often missed?
questions.why: The quiet, withdrawn patient is labelled tired or depressed. Screening every shift with a structured tool is what finds it.

questions.q: What most reliably distinguishes delirium from dementia at the bedside?
questions.a: Acute onset and fluctuation, with impaired attention
questions.why: Dementia is gradual and attention is relatively spared until late. The two coexist often: dementia is the strongest risk factor for delirium.

questions.q: Which are common, correctable causes of delirium in a hospitalised older patient?
questions.why: Drugs, hypoxia, dehydration, sodium and glucose disturbances, and withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines complete the list. A bladder scan and a rectal examination are not optional.

questions.q: Which drug classes most often precipitate delirium?
questions.why: Diphenhydramine, oxybutynin and tricyclics are the anticholinergics that catch people out. The medication list is reviewed against the Beers criteria on day one.

questions.q: What is the first-line management of delirium once the cause is being treated?
questions.a: Non-drug measures: reorientation, sleep, glasses and hearing aids, mobility, family presence
questions.why: Multicomponent programmes prevent about a third of cases and shorten the rest. No drug has been shown to prevent delirium.

questions.q: When is an antipsychotic justified in delirium?
questions.a: Severe agitation that endangers the patient or others, at the lowest dose for the shortest time
d: For hypoactive delirium to improve alertness
questions.why: Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium and carry stroke and QT risks in older patients. Low-dose haloperidol or an atypical is used, with an ECG.

questions.q: In which single situation are benzodiazepines the right treatment for delirium?
questions.why: Everywhere else they deepen and prolong delirium. Withdrawal delirium is the exception because the benzodiazepine treats the cause.

questions.q: Which sleep aid should not be given to an older hospitalised patient?
d: A quiet, dark room at night
questions.why: It is strongly anticholinergic. Sleep hygiene on the ward, with lights and noise down at night and daylight and activity by day, is the intervention with evidence.

questions.q: When is neuroimaging indicated in a patient with delirium?
questions.a: Focal neurological signs, head trauma, anticoagulation, or no cause found on initial work-up
d: Only if the patient is under 65
questions.why: Most delirium has a systemic cause found on examination, bloods, glucose, oxygen and the drug chart. Routine scanning of every confused patient rarely changes management.

questions.q: A family asks how long the confusion will last. What is an honest answer?
questions.a: Days to weeks, and sometimes longer; some patients never fully return to baseline
d: It resolves within 24 hours of treating the cause
It only lasts while in hospital
questions.why: Delirium is linked to longer stays, institutionalisation, later dementia and death. That is why prevention is taken as seriously as treatment.

questions.q: Which of these increases delirium rather than preventing it?
d: Reorientation with a clock and calendar
questions.why: Restraints raise agitation, injury and immobility. A sitter or family member at the bedside is the safer alternative for a patient at risk of pulling lines.
